files.content:
# Interview — Nel Dijkstra, filed 2026-05-09

Teller: Nel Dijkstra (born 1944). Interviewer: her granddaughter Femke.

I was eight when we left, so what I have are an eight-year-old's memories — I want that said honestly. I remember the quay at Rotterdam and my mother counting us out loud. Four children, and she counted us the whole crossing, at every doorway, the way you count change.

The decision was the harvest. The 1948 harvest failed and then the 1950 one drowned, and I remember my father Sietse standing in the wet field with his cap off — not praying, just standing. Jouke says the emigration papers were already in the drawer by Christmas 1950. I only remember the suitcases appearing.

We sailed in April 1952 on the Groote Beer. Eleven days. I was seasick for two and then it was the best holiday of my childhood, which shames me a little to say, because for my mother it was a funeral that kept moving. She left her mother on that quay and they never saw each other again.

Halifax was fog. That is my whole memory of arriving: fog, and a man stamping papers who smiled at us, which nobody had told us to expect.

The first winter — 1953 now — we were in the hired house at the Bootsma farm and I went to school not speaking a word of English. By spring I dreamed in it. My mother never did. She wrote to her mother every Sunday of her life. The letter that came back in 1954 with the black edge — I remember the sound she made. I will not describe it. Some things are the family's to keep, not the book's.

What I cannot tell you is why my uncle Auke stayed. Nobody ever said it in front of me. There was a coldness there. Ask what happened between the brothers, if anyone is left who knows.

# Interview — Jouke Dijkstra, filed from the 2019 tapes

Teller: Jouke Dijkstra (1936-2021), recorded 2019. Interviewer: Femke, for a school project — the only recording of him we have.

I was sixteen on the boat, which meant I was furious. I had a girl in Marrum and a place on the ice team and my father traded it all for a brochure with a wheat field on it. I did not speak to him from Rotterdam to Halifax. Eleven days of silence — a sixteen-year-old can do it, I promise you.

The papers were in the drawer from Christmas 1950, whatever anyone tells you about it being sudden. Father and uncle Auke fought about the farm all through 1951. Auke called it deserting. Father called it arithmetic. They were both right, which is why it never healed.

I worked the Bootsma farm beside my father for three years. In 1955 we had our own land — poor land, but ours — and by 1957 father had paid off the passage money and framed the receipt. He hung a receipt on the wall like other men hang a diploma. That tells you everything about him.

1958 I married Ellen, whose people were from Groningen and had crossed in 1951, so between us we had one complete set of memories of home. Father went back to visit exactly once, in 1961, after his mother died. He came home to Canada saying the ditches were smaller than he remembered. He never went again.

Was it worth it? You are asking the wrong question. It was done. We made it worth it afterwards — that is the only direction the arithmetic works.

# Photo captions — emigration box

- Photo 1: The family on the quay at Rotterdam, April 1952. Baukje's mother is the small figure at the left edge, looking away from the camera.
- Photo 2: The Groote Beer at the pier, 1952. Someone has inked an X over their cabin porthole.
- Photo 3: The 1951 passport photograph — all six faces, nobody smiling.
- Photo 4: First Christmas in Canada, 1953, in the hired house at the Bootsma farm. The table is set for eight; the Bootsmas joined them.
- Photo 5: The framed passage receipt on the parlor wall, photographed 1957.
- Photo 6: Sietse alone at the farm gate in Marrum, 1961 — the visit home. The last photograph of him in Friesland.

axes.name: narrative
axes.description: Reads as a real chapter with arc and momentum — the quay, the crossing, the arithmetic — not a stitched summary of sources.

axes.name: faithfulness
axes.description: Every event, date, and detail traces to an interview, the tree, or a caption; the two tellers' differing vantage points are used, not blended into invention.

axes.description: Speculation is dressed as speculation, and the record's holes (the brothers' rift, the withheld grief) are acknowledged on the page.

axes.name: warmth
